name: WrenJIT
baseline: LuaJIT 2.1 (version and build flags not stated)
workload: Nine small paired kernels, each written once in Wren and once in Lua (sum, range for, fib, tak, ack, mutual recursion, deep recursion, binary trees, method call); the Wren timer includes JIT warmup and compilation, process startup excluded; best of five self-timed runs.
claimed_speedup: WrenJIT time versus LuaJIT time (lower is better): sum 0.641 ms vs 1.092 ms (0.59x), range for 0.074 ms vs 0.584 ms (0.13x), fib 39.4 ms vs 51.9 ms (0.76x), tak 2.224 ms vs 6.361 ms (0.35x), ack 0.024 ms vs 1.066 ms (0.02x), mutual recursion 0.098 ms vs 0.321 ms (0.31x), deep recursion 0.625 ms vs 6.724 ms (0.09x), binary trees 8.807 ms vs 19.8 ms (0.45x), method call 0.087 ms vs 0.448 ms (0.19x).
compiler_and_flags: CMake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release with a C99 compiler (compiler not named); SLJIT backend; pinned Wren 99d2f0b and sljit d9902b1; LuaJIT build and flags not stated
tradeoffs: Only runs Wren programs (a patched Wren VM, patches/0001-wren-jit-hooks.patch). One trace per loop PC, no side traces or trace chaining. Recursion is compiled by recognising complete bytecode shapes and emitting native kernels, not by a general method JIT. Tested on ARM64 and x86-64 only.
caveats: The README itself says these are 'narrow kernels, not a language-wide victory lap'. The recursive wins (ack 0.02x, tak, mutual recursion, deep recursion) come from shape-matched native kernels for those exact programs, so they say little about general Wren code. Sub-millisecond timings on several rows. The two programs are separate ports in two languages, so the comparison depends on how equivalent the Lua versions are. The LuaJIT version is not stated. The 'full report' page on a github.io host was not opened (host blocked in this environment). Single first-party author, 4 stars, repo started 2026-02-22.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/tracing-jit topic page (WrenJIT listed, 4 stars)

name: Objeck
baseline: LuaJIT 2.1 (tracing JIT); the same table also lists Java 21 (OpenJDK 21.0.12 HotSpot, tiered JIT), CPython 3.12.3 and Ruby 3.2.3
workload: Computer Language Benchmarks Game programs (nbody 50M, binarytrees 17, spectralnorm 5500, fannkuchredux 12) in one Docker run, median of 3 runs; Objeck programs compiled with -opt s3 and JIT-compiled at runtime.
claimed_speedup: fannkuchredux 12: Objeck 32.76 s vs LuaJIT 117.99 s (the page says 3.6x faster) and Java 21 20.70 s (Java faster); binarytrees 17: Objeck 2.14 s vs LuaJIT 3.57 s (Java 0.26 s); but nbody 50M: Objeck 8.14 s vs LuaJIT 4.37 s and spectralnorm 5500: Objeck 2.72 s vs LuaJIT 1.12 s (LuaJIT faster). Java wins 3 of the 4 rows.
compiler_and_flags: Objeck v2026.9.1 (f6b3b09046) built from source with its standard libraries rebuilt by the same compiler, programs compiled with -opt s3; Ubuntu 24.04.4 in Docker (perf-results/docker/Dockerfile, which installs LuaJIT from the distro apt package 'luajit')
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 7950X3D (16C/32T), 128 GB RAM (62 GB visible in Docker), Docker on a Windows 11 host
tradeoffs: A separate language (Objeck), not a drop-in for Lua or Java code. Method JIT applies to methods annotated native and to auto-JIT for methods containing MTHD_CALL. binarytrees peaks at 209 MB RSS against single-digit MB for the others. Interpreter-bound rows run 30-50% slower in Docker than natively, per the page.
caveats: Only four benchmarks appear in the cross-language table and Objeck loses to LuaJIT on two of them and to Java on three. The LuaJIT fannkuchredux time (117.99 s) is unusually long compared with Objeck's 32.76 s and Java's 20.70 s; the Lua source used was not inspected, so the LuaJIT row may reflect a naive port. LuaJIT is the distro package, exact build not stated. The most recent commit seen was a bot download-stats snapshot, with release v2026.9.7 also referenced on the repo page.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/jit-compilation topic page (objeck-lang listed), then docs/performance.md

name: Wangshu (Lua 5.1 VM with method JIT)
baseline: gopher-lua (the common Go Lua 5.1 VM). LuaJIT is named only as an aspiration and no LuaJIT numbers are given.
workload: Pure-Lua micro kernels and five Benchmarks Game scripts run inside the embedded VM, median of 3 runs of 2 s at one CPU, on the same CI runner as the gopher-lua baseline; tiers P1 interpreter, P3 wasm layer, P4 method JIT.
claimed_speedup: P4 (method JIT) vs gopher-lua on linux/amd64: HeavyArith 15.7 ms vs 292 ms (18.5x), HeavyFloatloop 25.7 ms vs 464 ms (18.0x), HeavyRecursion 1.89 ms vs 9.34 ms (4.93x), fib 1.09 ms vs 10.2 ms (9.35x), spectral-norm 2.40 ms vs 37.0 ms (15.4x), n-body 4.64 ms vs 68.4 ms (14.7x), fannkuch 0.62 ms vs 4.87 ms (7.87x), binary-trees 29.7 ms vs 56.0 ms (1.89x); the interpreter tier alone is 3-5.5x on simple micro kernels.
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.27+ (go.mod 1.27.0); go test -bench with -benchtime=2s -count=3 -cpu=1, median; P3/P4 tiers selected by build tags; GitHub Actions workflow bench-readme-table (2026-07-10)
hardware: linux/amd64: Intel Xeon Platinum 8573C (GitHub-hosted runner); also linux/arm64 Azure Cobalt 100 and darwin/arm64 Apple M-series (macos-latest) in the same README
stars_or_usage: 8 stars; the README says it runs in production at the author's company
tradeoffs: Pure Go, no cgo. Lua 5.1 core only (no VARARG in compiled tiers, io.open/popen missing, debug library partial). The Go-to-Lua call boundary is slower than gopher-lua (CallOnly 0.47x for the interpreter, 0.41x for P4 on amd64; Boundary 0.56x/0.63x), recovering only with the zero-allocation CallInto API. The P4 tier is marked release-candidate and a trace JIT tier (P5) is not yet implemented.
caveats: The baseline is gopher-lua, not LuaJIT, PyPy, V8 or HotSpot; the README says it aims at LuaJIT-class speed but publishes no LuaJIT comparison. Numbers come from a shared hosted runner (README warns of 10-20% drift and tells readers to use ratios). The CI run page cited in the README was not opened. The README is mainly in Chinese (an English README exists). The 18x rows are numeric kernels the JIT is designed for, and the README notes the P3 wasm tier is slower than the interpreter on several rows.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/lua-vm topic page (wangshu listed), confirmed on github.com/topics/jit?l=go

name: Luava
baseline: LuaJ 3.0.1 (the widely used Java Lua implementation); PUC Lua and LuaJIT are not benchmarked
workload: Ten Lua tasks (arithmetic loop, recursive fib, table insert/scan, string concat, closures, coroutines, hash table, OOP metatables, string patterns, sieve), paired interleaved runs against LuaJ, order-flipped, median, warm=6, iters=10, with -Dluava.jit.sync=true.
claimed_speedup: LuaJ time over Luava time: coroutines 234.7 ms vs 4549.9 ms (19.39x), recursive fib 243.8 ms vs 2538.6 ms (10.41x), arithmetic loop 33.7 ms vs 285.6 ms (8.47x), string concat 3.03x, table insert/scan 2.83x, hash table 2.68x, sieve 1.84x, string patterns 1.43x, closures 1.21x, OOP metatables 1.21x; all 10 tasks won.
compiler_and_flags: JDK 21+; -Dluava.jit.sync=true (synchronous JIT compilation); other JVM flags not stated
tradeoffs: Pure-Java Lua 5.4 (register bytecode VM with a tiered JIT, sandboxing with instruction limits, Java interop). Requires JDK 21+. MPL-2.0 is file-level copyleft.
caveats: First-party numbers with no hardware stated. The baseline LuaJ interprets Lua 5.2 semantics, while Luava implements 5.4, so the tasks are not exactly equivalent. The README says what remains between Luava and PUC Lua (C) is dispatch cost, so it is probably still slower than C Lua and LuaJIT; neither is measured. Synchronous JIT mode is used for the benchmark, which removes background-compile effects. Very small project (52 commits, 2 stars).

name: musql
baseline: SQLite (C, via mattn/go-sqlite3); Turso's Go driver is also compared
workload: Read queries over 100,000 rows on disk-backed files with a warm cache, each checked against C SQLite on 40 bind values before timing, then timed for about 200 ms; musql run with and without its JIT (MUSQL_JIT=0).
claimed_speedup: Apple M4, JIT vs C SQLite: filtered count with one predicate 28 us vs 2.17 ms (77x), two predicates 92x, sum over a filter 8.5x, grouped aggregate 2.1x, ORDER BY v DESC LIMIT 20 2.7x, whole-table count 1.8x. Intel Xeon D-2123IT: 70x, 65x, 7.6x, 2.4x, 2.0x, 1.6x. Slower rows: rowid lookup 1.8x slower on the Xeon (1.0x on M4), secondary-index equality 1.2x/2.9x slower, indexed equi-join 1.3x slower on the Xeon.
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.27.0 (go.mod); harness compat-harness/bench_columnar_vs_c_test.go (TestBenchColumnarVsC); JIT on vs MUSQL_JIT=0; C SQLite through cgo
hardware: Apple M4 (arm64, macOS) and Intel Xeon D-2123IT (amd64, Linux)
tradeoffs: SQLite-compatible SQL on a new columnar .musq segment format with an append-only delta; import/export tools to and from SQLite files. The JIT covers only supported scan/filter/aggregate query paths; point lookups and joins do not use it. Pure Go driver, but the benchmark harness needs cgo.
caveats: The win comes from columnar storage plus JIT against SQLite's row store; without the JIT musql is much slower than C SQLite on the same scans (for example 9.83 ms vs 2.17 ms for the one-predicate filtered count on M4). Read workloads only; writes, updates and deletes are skipped in the published harness run (BENCH_SKIP). Microsecond-scale rows vary run to run, more on amd64. The headline 75x is an average over two machines of the best rows. Go toolchain build flags are defaults and not otherwise stated.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/jit?l=go&o=desc&s=updated topic page (musql listed, '75x C SQLite performance')

name: katsu
baseline: Node.js 26.8.1 (V8); Bun 1.4.0 and Deno 2.9.6 are also measured
workload: Cold start of a one-line console.log program (median of 25 runs after 3 discarded, hyperfine-style harness katsu-bench), plus peak RSS and binary size.
claimed_speedup: Cold start: katsu 0.0.5 1.55 ms vs Node 24.63 ms (the page says 15.9x faster), Bun 4.97 ms (3.2x), Deno 12.49 ms; peak RSS 2.44 MiB vs 48.14 MiB for Node; binary 1.7 MiB vs 139.0 MiB for Node. Compute is a loss: the katsu README gives fib(35) at 875 ms vs 53.4 ms on Node (16.4x slower, as of v0.1.6) and the katsu-bench README (https://github.com/tamnd/katsu-bench, also opened) shows fib 20-25x behind Bun.
compiler_and_flags: katsu built with cargo build --release, later runs from the published tarball; runtimes at latest releases of 2026-08-28; flags for the others not stated
hardware: Apple M4 (10 cores, 24 GB), macOS 15.8 (laptop, turbo on, frequency scaling on)
tradeoffs: Pre-alpha JavaScript/TypeScript runtime in Rust that plans a three-tier engine with a copy-and-patch baseline JIT. No module system, event loop, filesystem or standard library beyond console.log at the time of measurement. 12.31% of test262 passing at v0.1.8.
caveats: The author states the lead exists 'because it does less, not because it is better'. The measured binary is an interpreter with an inline cache, not yet a JIT, and compute is 16-25x slower than Node and Bun. Numbers are the project's own, from a laptop with turbo on and are labelled 'indicative' in the spec. Included mainly as a startup and footprint claim against V8-based Node.
found_via: WebSearch: github JavaScript engine JIT faster than V8 benchmark (katsu spec/15-benchmarks.md surfaced), then tamnd/katsu and tamnd/katsu-bench

name: Perry
baseline: Node.js v25.8.0 (V8); Bun 1.3.12 and Java OpenJDK 21.0.7 (HotSpot) appear in the same table
workload: Polyglot sweep of nine identical f64 benchmarks (fibonacci, loop_overhead, loop_data_dependent, array_write, array_read, math_intensive, object_create, nested_loops, accumulate), median of 11 runs; Perry compiles the same TypeScript source that Node and Bun run.
claimed_speedup: Perry default vs Node: fibonacci 309 ms vs 987 ms (3.2x, derived from page data) vs Bun 518 ms vs Java 278 ms; array_write 3 ms vs 9 ms; object_create 2 ms vs 8 ms; accumulate 97 ms vs 597 ms. Perry loses on loop_overhead (97 ms vs Node 53 ms, Bun 41 ms), roughly ties nested_loops (18 ms vs Node 17 ms), and the README shows the 500k-record JSON pipeline at 1,649 ms vs Node 1,010 ms and Bun 647 ms. A second report in the repo quotes image convolution at 268 ms for Perry with Node 4.5x slower.
compiler_and_flags: Perry v0.5.908 (LLVM backend), default mode without fast-math; METHODOLOGY.md lists rustc -O, clang++ -O3, javac and java (HotSpot JIT), Node v25.8.0 run on precompiled JS, Bun 1.3.12; no non-default optimization flags
hardware: Apple M1 Max (10 cores, 64 GB RAM), macOS 26.4; the separate honest_bench report used an x86_64 16-core Ubuntu 24.04 machine
tradeoffs: Ahead-of-time compiler, not a JIT: compiles a typed TypeScript subset to native executables through SWC and LLVM, with Node-compatible shims (about 97% of Node's own test suite passes on 53 node:* modules per the README). No dynamic eval. Binaries are 330 KB and up, with lower RSS than Node.
caveats: This is an AOT compiler measured against V8's JIT, included because the claim is against Node/V8. Results are mixed and the repo says so; HotSpot Java is faster on fibonacci. The METHODOLOGY.md lists Perry v0.5.585 while RESULTS.md reports v0.5.908, so the methodology file is stale. The separate honest_bench REPORT.md is internally inconsistent: its bottom line says Perry 268 ms on image convolution (4.5x faster than Node) while a table further down in the same file lists Perry 1,204 ms vs Node 975 ms. Written by the project itself with a 'we publish everything' framing. The README table highlights favourable rows.
found_via: WebFetch: github.com/PerryTS/perry (named as a comparable AOT project in tamnd/katsu spec/15-benchmarks.md)

name: Graal compiler (GraalVM JIT)
baseline: HotSpot C2 JIT (OpenJDK HotSpot VM, JDK 25)
workload: JMH suite from the ionutbalosin/jvm-performance-benchmarks repository on JDK 25 x86_64: 298 compiler-optimization microbenchmarks (inlining, loop unrolling, escape analysis, devirtualization and similar) and 1136 benchmarks overall including Java API and classic programs.
claimed_speedup: Normalized geometric mean of time per op (lower is better): compiler category C2 JIT 1.00 vs GraalVM CE JIT 0.84 and Oracle GraalVM JIT 0.84 over 298 benchmarks; whole suite OpenJDK HotSpot VM 1.0 vs GraalVM CE 0.9 and Oracle GraalVM 0.9 over 1136 benchmarks.
compiler_and_flags: JDK 25; JMH harness; GraalVM CE and Oracle GraalVM JIT vs OpenJDK HotSpot C2; JVM flags live in the suite's scripts and were not opened
stars_or_usage: 21.7k stars (oracle/graal); the benchmark suite ionutbalosin/jvm-performance-benchmarks has 132 stars
tradeoffs: The Graal JIT plugs into HotSpot through JVMCI, or ships inside GraalVM. GraalVM Community Edition is GPLv2 with Classpath Exception; the Oracle GraalVM build has separate licence terms, so only the CE numbers are about copyable code. Memory, warmup and startup are not covered by the geomean pages opened.
caveats: The numbers are in a third-party suite, not in the oracle/graal repo, whose README gives no performance figures. The CPU model is not stated on the pages opened (README covers OS tuning only), which is why this is tier B rather than A. The compiler category is made of handwritten patterns chosen to exercise optimizations, so the 16% geomean gap is not an application speedup. Normalized geometric means hide per-benchmark losses. The whole-suite figures (0.9 vs 1) are in the sibling file https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ionutbalosin/jvm-performance-benchmarks/HEAD/results/jdk-25/x86_64/geomean/summary.csv, which was also opened. The suite author's articles for JDK 17 and 21 (blog host) were not opened.
found_via: WebSearch: github JIT compiler faster than HotSpot OR outperforms HotSpot benchmark JVM (surfaced ionutbalosin/jvm-performance-benchmarks), then its results/jdk-25/x86_64/geomean CSV files

name: goja-perf
baseline: Upstream dop251/goja at merge base 8f1c069 (pure-Go JavaScript interpreter); V8 comparison suite exists but publishes no numbers
workload: 55 shared Go benchmarks from goja's suite, ten samples per version interleaved on Go 1.26.2, comparing fork commit 35cc441 with its upstream merge base; seven benchmarks improved significantly and none regressed significantly.
claimed_speedup: MainLoop 24.541 ms to 98.277 us (249.71x, bytes per op 5,598,185 to 324), CallJS 267.10 ns to 93.56 ns (2.86x), CallNative 191.60 ns to 92.67 ns (2.07x), VmNOP2 1.96x, FuncCall 1.81x, MapDelete 1.48x, CallReflect 1.39x.
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.26.2; go test benchmarks compared with benchstat-style significance; eligible integer loop traces compile to native code on Windows/amd64 and Linux/amd64, other platforms use a portable typed Go executor
tradeoffs: API-compatible fork that keeps the upstream package name and swaps the import path; adds adaptive quickening, typed traces with native code for supported numeric loop shapes, cheaper Go/JS boundary calls and an opt-in capability sandbox. Native traces cover only supported integer and float accumulation and counter loops.
caveats: The 249.71x headline is one micro benchmark (MainLoop, a counter-loop shape the trace compiler handles); the other significant rows are 1.4x-2.9x and the remaining 48 benchmarks did not change significantly. The repo's benchjs suite compares the same JS workloads with V8 but its results directory is gitignored, so there is no published V8 comparison; V8 would be far faster on compute. Independent fork with two stars, not an upstream goja release. Measured on one Windows laptop CPU.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/jit?l=go topic page (maclof/goja-perf listed as 'ECMAScript/JavaScript engine optimized for performance')

name: DIO-JIT
workload: Seven small Python programs (brainfuck interpreter, append3, DNA read, fib(15), hypot on strings, selection sort, trans), pure CPython versus the same code under the DIO-JIT decorator; units are not stated on the page.
claimed_speedup: fib(15): 11.63 vs 1.54 on Python 3.8 and 10.41 vs 1.51 on 3.9 (about 7x); trans 24.22 vs 7.79; append3 23.94 vs 10.70; BF 265.74 vs 134.23; selection sort 46.95 vs 33.88; DNA READ shows little gain (16.96 vs 14.82). The README also claims 500x on a partial-evaluation fib example.
tradeoffs: A JIT that runs inside CPython (3.8 and later, relies on LOAD_METHOD) and optimizes by type specialisation rules; users add @jit.jit decorators. The README says it is not production ready and many specialisation rules are still missing. Programs using bytearray and bytes see no gain.
caveats: No hardware, no units, no CPython build details, and no comparison with PyPy, which is the strong baseline for Python JIT speed. Only microbenchmarks, benchmark scripts are linked from the README but were not opened. Last commit 2021-02-18.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/python-jit topic page (thautwarm/restrain-jit and diojit), then the diojit README

name: JPHP
workload: Benchmark scripts run through './gradlew bench' on JPHP and 'php -f bench/src/bench.php' on PHP; the README states only the summary ratios.
claimed_speedup: README feature line: JIT (~2.5x faster PHP 5.6, ~1.1x faster PHP 7.0, ~13% slower than PHP 7.4).
tradeoffs: PHP 7.1+ language implementation on the JVM (PHP compiled to JVM bytecode and then JIT-compiled by the JVM), with Java interop, UTF-16 strings, threads and JavaFX/SWT GUI extensions. Not drop-in for PHP extensions.
caveats: Ratios only, no hardware or workload detail, and the README itself says it is slower than PHP 7.4 (the numbers predate PHP 8 and its JIT). Last commit 2020-07-07. Listed for completeness as a PHP-on-JVM claim, not as a win over PyPy, LuaJIT, V8 or HotSpot.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/jit?l=java topic page (jphp-group/jphp listed, 1.7k stars)

name: XS (xs-lang)
baseline: Node 20 (V8) and Python 3.13 (CPython), measured in the same README table
workload: Two programs run cold from disk: hello world (startup) and recursive fib(30); XS shown in --interp, --vm and --jit modes; best of three runs.
claimed_speedup: fib(30): XS --jit 31 ms vs Node 20 62 ms vs Python 3.13 71 ms (the --vm tier is 180 ms and --interp 950 ms); hello world startup: XS 3 ms vs Node 20 57 ms vs Python 3.13 15 ms.
hardware: Linux x86-64, AMD Ryzen 7 (exact model not stated)
tradeoffs: A new language shipped as one static binary with compiler, language server, formatter and package manager; compiles to native code, JavaScript or WebAssembly. The JIT compiles only the opcodes in its supported set and falls back to the VM for the rest, and is meant for profiled hotspots.
caveats: The README says 'treat as indicative, not authoritative'. One compute benchmark, a call-bound recursive fib that favours a simple JIT, and CPU model and compiler flags missing. The Node version is old (20). A reproduction script (tests/bench_backends.sh, 'xs bench') is named but was not opened. Not a drop-in for JavaScript or Python programs.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/jit?l=c&o=desc&s=updated and nearby topic pages (xs-lang0/xs listed), then its README Benchmarks section
